summary:
We developed an interactive web platform and analysis pipeline that transforms multi-epoch astronomical sky images into dynamic "blink videos" to detect, track, and verify moving celestial objects. Built for NASA’s SPHEREx mission data, archival surveys like WISE and Gaia, and custom FITS uploads, the platform enables users to smoothly animate time-series sky cutouts, perform real-time image subtraction, and use interactive split-screen swiping to immediately spot moving bodies against fixed background stars.

The platform addresses the challenges of cross-epoch tracking and false positives. When an object is selected, the system assigns a persistent identity across observation dates, calculates its true speed and direction across the sky, and extracts on-the-fly 102-band spectral curves and light curves. This ensures stationary variable stars fluctuating in brightness are not mistaken for moving objects and allows users to quickly verify candidates like cold brown dwarfs and asteroids.

This project is important because massive all-sky surveys produce vast volumes of data where manual inspection is a major bottleneck. By delivering research-grade astrometry, spectral verification, and shareable live links inside a zero-install browser interface, the platform accelerates discovery for professional astronomers, students, and citizen scientists alike.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

The SPHEREx Moving-Object & Trajectory Platform is a web-based astronomical application that helps users view, detect, and track moving celestial objects across sky images taken at different times. It is designed to work with multi-band data from NASA's SPHEREx mission, archive surveys like WISE and Gaia, and custom images uploaded by users.

How it works:

  • Image Ingestion & Alignment: Searches NASA archives for sky cutouts across SPHEREx's 102 wavelength channels (from near-infrared to mid-infrared) or accepts user-uploaded FITS image files. It automatically validates telescope coordinates and aligns the images so different dates match up precisely.
  • Interactive Blink Video: Displays aligned images in a responsive web viewer, playing through observation dates like a short video (from slow blinks to rapid playback). Users can also step through dates frame by frame to spot objects shifting position against fixed background stars.
  • Comparison & Swipe Tools: Lets users compare any two observation dates directly by subtracting one image from another, viewing pixel ratios, or dragging an interactive split-screen slider to reveal moving bodies and brightness changes immediately.
  • Object Tracking with Persistent Identity: Automatically detects bright candidate sources. Users can click on any object or draw a box around it to track it. The system assigns a persistent label (such as Track A or Track B) that stays with the object across all dates, even when observations are spaced months apart.
  • Motion Fitting & Spectral Analysis: Calculates the object's speed, direction of motion across the sky (proper motion), and distance-related shift (parallax). It also extracts an on-the-fly 102-channel spectral curve and light curve over time, helping determine whether the target is an asteroid, a cold brown dwarf, or a variable star.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Keeps Track of Objects Across Dates: Solves the common problem where a moving object loses its track identity between observations taken on different days or years.
  • Tells Moving Objects Apart from Variable Stars: Prevents false alarms by checking whether a candidate is genuinely changing position or simply changing brightness (like pulsating variable stars).
  • Brings Images and Spectra Together: Allows researchers to inspect both the visual movement and the multi-wavelength spectrum in one place without needing separate programs.
  • Zero Software Installation: Runs entirely inside modern web browsers, eliminating the need to install specialized astronomical software suites on personal computers.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Accelerating Discoveries in Space: Helps identify near-Earth asteroids, distant solar system bodies, and cold brown dwarfs in upcoming large-scale sky surveys.
  • Making Astronomy Data Accessible: Makes inspecting multi-epoch telescope images and calculating motion accessible to professional astronomers, students, and citizen scientists alike.
  • Encouraging Scientific Accuracy: Supplies clear uncertainty estimates and flags for camera artifacts, ensuring automated detections are checked responsibly before being claimed as real discoveries.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, SQL, HTML, CSS.
  • Astronomy & Math Libraries: Astropy (celestial coordinate alignment and time standards), Photutils (background estimation and star detection), Astroquery (NASA IRSA, Gaia, and solar system database queries), Reproject, SciPy, and NumPy.
  • Backend Framework: FastAPI (API server), Pydantic (data validation), SQLAlchemy and Alembic (database management).
  • Database & Task Queues: PostgreSQL (storing project metadata and spatial indexing), Redis (caching and request management), and Celery (background image processing).
  • Frontend & Visualization: React, Vite, Zustand (application state), TanStack Query, WebGL2 and Canvas (high-performance image playback and comparison slider), and Aladin Lite (deep-sky integration).
  • Infrastructure & Testing: Docker and Docker Compose for deployment, Pytest for backend testing, and Vitest for frontend unit tests.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Modernizing the Astronomical Blink Comparator: Upgrades the century-old astronomical technique of blinking photo plates into a smooth, interactive browser video with live image subtraction and split-screen swiping.
  • Real-Time Sky and Spectrum HUD: Translates screen pixels into true sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination) and detector wavelengths directly under the user's mouse cursor in real time.
  • One-Click Motion and Spectrum Inspection: Instead of treating images and spectra as separate workflows, clicking a moving candidate immediately plots both its flight path across the sky and its 102-channel spectral signature.
  • Shareable Live Views: Lets users share their exact findings, coordinates, and viewing state via simple web links or embed them directly into external websites and research articles.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Preserving Measurement Accuracy: Conducted all motion and position calculations on the original telescope coordinates rather than distorted screen pixels.
  • Handling False Alarms and Artifacts: Built automatic alerts for camera flaws, such as cosmic ray strikes, saturated pixels, and edge effects, so noise is not mistaken for a new discovery.
  • Testing with Real Benchmark Targets: Validated the system against well-known astronomical calibration targets—including Barnard's Star (a very fast-moving star), WISE 0855 (a cold brown dwarf), and known variable stars (RW Aurigae and R Draconis) to ensure stationary fluctuating stars are not misclassified as movers.
  • Web Speed and Large File Handling: Used lightweight WebP image previews, background job queues, and caching so large telescope files (up to 200 MB) load smoothly without freezing the browser.
  • Ease of Use and Accessibility: Designed with a clean layout, keyboard shortcuts (such as the spacebar to play or pause the blink video and arrow keys to step frames), and high-contrast sky views.
